catalog_quote: Stress is defined as loudness and duration. In this study, stress is predictable from its position in a word and from the syllabic structure. Accordingly, no stress mark is written in phonemic transcription. The strongly stressed syllable (with all types of syllabic structure except CVᵀ) always occupies the last position, and the weakly stressed syllable (with syllabic structure CV(:)(C)ᵀ) and the unstressed syllable (with syllabic structure CVᵀ) precede the strongly stressed syllable in the poly-syllabic words. [p. 57] ... Word stress in Phuan can be mentioned in four types: in monosyllabic word, in disyllabic word, in trisyllabic word, and in quadrisyllabic word. 2.3.1 In a monosyllabic word, which has only one syllable, the strong stress is on that syllable. It has only one structure: S. [p. 58] ... 3.3.1 Nuclear Syllable. This is the stressed syllable (or the strongly stressed syllable which functions as nucleus of the phonological word. It always occupies the final position in poly-syllabic word. The syllable can be an open syllable or a closed syllable. [p. 69]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and predictable: the last syllable of every word carries the strong stress (monosyllables are simply stressed); all preceding syllables in polysyllabic words are either weakly stressed (any full syllable CV(:)(C) with tone) or unstressed (a CV presyllable with short vowel and tone, e.g. ka-, ta-, sa-). Attested patterns: US, WS; WUS, WWS; UWUS, UWWS, WWWS.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Three degrees are distinguished: strong (S), weak (W) and unstressed (U). Weakly stressed syllables are full syllables in non-final position; unstressed syllables are minor CV presyllables (open, short vowel). Both may occupy first or penultimate position (§3.3.2, pp. 69-70).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the only restriction is that a CVᵀ (short open) syllable cannot be the strongly stressed one, so it never occurs word-finally. Polysyllabic examples include loans/compounds (e.g. 'brass ladle', 'policeman', 'measles').
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word in isolation (citation forms elicited from informants at Ban Hat Siaw, Sukhothai); Phuan is tonal (Eam-eium's numbered tones 1-9 marked on every syllable) and stress is described alongside tone as a predictable positional property. Two Thai-language Silpakorn theses on Lao Phuan in Nakhon Nayok (Sungvanthrup 1991: 86) and Prachinburi (Sukpiti 1989: 57) independently state that in true disyllables the first syllable is 'lighter or shorter' than the second, consistent with final prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Eam-eium 1986 describes the Phuan of Ban Hat Siaw, Tambon Hat Siaw, Si Satchanalai district, Sukhothai province (Thailand) — a Thai-side Phuan community descended from 19th-century resettlement from Xiang Khouang, Laos; Glottolog has no separate dialect code, so it falls under phua1239. The corroborating Silpakorn theses describe Lao Phuan of Nong Saeng (Nakhon Nayok) and Hua Wa (Prachinburi).

tone_statements.translation: In Phuan (Fai Mun) there are altogether 6 tones, namely: Tone 1 is low-rising /23/, occurring in box A1; Tone 2 is mid-rising /35/, occurring in A234 and DS123; Tone 3 is low level /22/, occurring in B123, DL123 and DS4; Tone 4 is mid-falling /31/, occurring in B4 and DL4; Tone 5 is mid level with glottal constriction at the end /33ˀ/, occurring in C1; and Tone 6 is high-falling with glottal constriction at the end /41ˀ/, occurring in C234.
tone_statements.locator: p. 19, section 4.2.1 ระบบวรรณยุกต์ในภาษาพวน, paragraph after Fig. 1
tone_statements.summary: Six tones in Fai Mun Phuan from the author's own fieldwork (auditory + Praat), shown in Gedney tone boxes; most Phuan varieties merge B=DL; Tanprasert 2003 groups Thai Phuan into 5- and 6-tone sets.

tone_statements.quote: The phoneme inventory in this Phuan dialect comprises tones, consonants and vowels. ... Tones. There are six tones; their phonetic characteristics are as follows. Tone 1 (T1) represents a low-rising pitch (24). ... Tone 2 (T2) represents a high-level pitch slightly falling at the end (443). ... Tone 3 (T3) represents a mid-falling pitch (32). ... Tone 4 (T4) represents a mid-level pitch and falling at the end (332). ... Tone 5 (T5) represents a high-level pitch with glottal closure (44ʔ). ... Tone 6 (T6)represents a high-rising pitch with glottal closure (45ʔ).
tone_statements.locator: Appendix 'Phoneme Inventory of Pong Ro Phuan', pp. 160-161; tone box also in Figure 2, p. 149
tone_statements.summary: Six tones (24, 443, 32, 332, 44ʔ, 45ʔ) via Gedney's checklist with two elderly speakers, shapes by the author's ear; checked-syllable allotones 35/44/42; B123=DL123, B4=DL4. Nothing on stress.

tone_statements.translation: As for tones, Phuan in its various localities differs in tone system and in the phonetic shape of the tones more than in the consonant or vowel system ... Considering the tone systems of all 13 Phuan localities so far researched, one sees that the tone-system data differ in some respects ... 1. Number of tonemes: each Phuan locality has a different number of tonemes, namely from 5 up to 8 tonemes, and they can be grouped as follows.
tone_statements.locator: p.71, paragraph below the vowel chart; and p.78, right column, section ๑. จำนวนหน่วยเสียงวรรณยุกต์
tone_statements.summary: Compares tone charts of 13 Phuan localities from earlier studies: 5-8 tonemes by locality, 9 of 13 have six; 7-8-tone counts add checked-syllable tones (p.79); labels = chart 12 p.77; no stress.

tone_statements.translation: 5.5 Tones in Lao Phuan. Lao Phuan has 5 tone phonemes as follows: T1 (lower-mid rising), T2 (mid level or mid falling-rising), T3 (lower-mid level), T4 (upper-mid falling), T5 (upper-mid rising with glottal closure). 5.5.1 The lower-mid rising tone (24) is a tone phoneme that starts at pitch level 2 and glides up to level 4 (see fig. 54).
tone_statements.locator: ch.5, sec. 5.5, thesis p.82; tone values 5.5.1-5.5.5 pp.82-85, fig. 60 tone-box chart p.85
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Phuan of Tha Tako: 5 tones, 24, 33~323, 22, 42, 45ʔ; proto-Tai boxes A1-234, B=DL, C unsplit. English abstract: 'Song has 6 tones, whereas the others have only 5 tones.' Nothing on stress.

tone.locator: p. 19, section 4.2.1 ระบบวรรณยุกต์ในภาษาพวน, paragraph after Fig. 1
tone.translation: In Phuan (Fai Mun) there are altogether 6 tones, namely: Tone 1 is low-rising /23/, occurring in box A1; Tone 2 is mid-rising /35/, occurring in A234 and DS123; Tone 3 is low level /22/, occurring in B123, DL123 and DS4; Tone 4 is mid-falling /31/, occurring in B4 and DL4; Tone 5 is mid level with glottal constriction at the end /33ˀ/, occurring in C1; and Tone 6 is high-falling with glottal constriction at the end /41ˀ/, occurring in C234.
tone.summary: Six tones in Fai Mun Phuan from the author's own fieldwork (auditory + Praat), shown in Gedney tone boxes; most Phuan varieties merge B=DL; Tanprasert 2003 groups Thai Phuan into 5- and 6-tone sets.

sources.quote: The phoneme inventory in this Phuan dialect comprises tones, consonants and vowels. ... Tones. There are six tones; their phonetic characteristics are as follows. Tone 1 (T1) represents a low-rising pitch (24). ... Tone 2 (T2) represents a high-level pitch slightly falling at the end (443). ... Tone 3 (T3) represents a mid-falling pitch (32). ... Tone 4 (T4) represents a mid-level pitch and falling at the end (332). ... Tone 5 (T5) represents a high-level pitch with glottal closure (44ʔ). ... Tone 6 (T6)represents a high-rising pitch with glottal closure (45ʔ).
sources.locator: Appendix 'Phoneme Inventory of Pong Ro Phuan', pp. 160-161; tone box also in Figure 2, p. 149
sources.note: Six tones (24, 443, 32, 332, 44ʔ, 45ʔ) via Gedney's checklist with two elderly speakers, shapes by the author's ear; checked-syllable allotones 35/44/42; B123=DL123, B4=DL4. Nothing on stress.

sources.quote: สำหรับเสียงวรรณยุกต์นั้นภาษาพวนในถิ่นต่างๆ จะมีระบบวรรณยุกต์และสัทลักษณะของวรรณยุกต์ต่างกันมากกว่าระบบพยัญชนะหรือสระ ... เมื่อพิจารณาระบบวรรณยุกต์ของภาษาพวนทั้ง ๑๓ ถิ่น เท่าที่มีผู้ทำวิจัยไว้ จะเห็นว่าข้อมูลระบบเสียงวรรณยุกต์มีความแตกต่างกันบางประการ ... ๑. จำนวนหน่วยเสียงวรรณยุกต์ภาษาพวนแต่ละถิ่นมีจำนวนหน่วยเสียงแตกต่างกัน กล่าวคือ มีตั้งแต่ ๕ หน่วยเสียง จนถึง ๘ หน่วยเสียง สามารถแบ่งเป็นกลุ่มได้ ดังนี้

tone.translation: As for tones, Phuan in its various localities differs in tone system and in the phonetic shape of the tones more than in the consonant or vowel system ... Considering the tone systems of all 13 Phuan localities so far researched, one sees that the tone-system data differ in some respects ... 1. Number of tonemes: each Phuan locality has a different number of tonemes, namely from 5 up to 8 tonemes, and they can be grouped as follows.

tone.translation: 5.5 Tones in Lao Phuan. Lao Phuan has 5 tone phonemes as follows: T1 (lower-mid rising), T2 (mid level or mid falling-rising), T3 (lower-mid level), T4 (upper-mid falling), T5 (upper-mid rising with glottal closure). 5.5.1 The lower-mid rising tone (24) is a tone phoneme that starts at pitch level 2 and glides up to level 4 (see fig. 54).

sources.quote: 1.4 A tone system catalogue We now present a catalogue of tone systems from most of the recorded Central and SWT languages. The reader will note the great variety of systems in the Lao-Southern Thai subgroup, while there is less in the Neua-Phuan and still less in the P group. ... Another interesting tendancy is the B 4 = C 123 = DL 4 coalescence found sporadically in certain Neua-Phuan languages as well as in some P languages (19, 24, 25, 30, 31, 35). ... PH - *BCD 123-4 ... 19. Pak Seng (Phuan) A B C DL DS ... 21. Phuan Lopburi A B C DL DS
